papers.title: Anorectal function after transanal natural orifice specimen extraction for colorectal cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Chua M, Lee A, Palanisamy P, Wee I, Seow-En I
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: Natural orifice specimen extraction (NOSE) eliminates the abdominal extraction incision after minimally invasive (MIS) colorectal resection and offers favourable short-term recovery, but transanal extraction raises concerns regarding sphincter stretch and anorectal dysfunction. This review evaluated anorectal functional outcomes after transanal NOSE compared with transabdominal specimen extraction (TASE) in MIS colorectal cancer surgery.
METHODS: MEDLINE and EMBASE were searched from inception to August 2024 for comparative studies reporting postoperative anorectal or pelvic floor functional outcomes following transanal NOSE versus TASE. The primary outcome was anorectal continence at the postoperative interval closest to 6 months.
RESULTS: Ten retrospective cohort studies were included, of which seven (1362 patients) contributed quantitative data for meta-analysis. Three studies contributed to the pooled Wexner incontinence score analysis and four to the pooled Pelvic Floor Distress Inventory short form (PFDI-20) analysis. At the interval closest to 6 months, Wexner scores were numerically higher after transanal NOSE than TASE, but the difference was small and non-significant (MD 0.17, 95% CI - 0.01 to 0.35; p = 0.07). PFDI-20 scores did not differ between groups (MD - 0.02, 95% CI - 0.21 to 0.18; p = 0.86). Both estimates were robust in leave-one-out and overlap-adjusted analyses excluding potentially overlapping Harbin Medical University cohorts. Early differences appeared to diminish over time, with no clear separation beyond 12 months.
CONCLUSION: Transanal NOSE was associated with a small, non-significant trend toward higher early Wexner scores after MIS colorectal cancer surgery, while broader pelvic floor symptom burden appeared comparable to TASE. The difference was of uncertain clinical significance, was robust to sensitivity analyses, and longer-term data suggested no persistent functional disadvantage.

papers.title: Design and outcome measures of clinical trials for active ulcerative colitis: a scoping review based on databases
papers.authors: Zhao X, Feng C, Zhao C, Zhang R, Zhang S, Wang R
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ulcerative colitis (UC) reduces the quality of life for patients and creates a significant economic burden on global healthcare systems. Although there have been advances in UC clinical trials recently, most existing reviews have primarily focused on pathogenesis or pharmacological treatments. This review analyzed the characteristics of current clinical trials for active ulcerative colitis and assessed research methods. This review focused on refining trial design and providing evidence-based methods for improving treatment outcomes and prognosis.
METHOD: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The study searched clinical trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR) from April 1, 2016, to April 1, 2026. In addition, the study searched PubMed for clinical trials published between April 1, 2016, and April 1, 2026. Data were charted and presented in tables.
RESULT: The study revealed a rapid increase in the number of clinical trials focusing on active ulcerative colitis since 2019. Biologics and small-molecule targeted drugs have become the core interventions, while traditional therapies constitute a smaller proportion of all treatments. However, these studies face limitations, such as small sample sizes, short follow-up periods, and an imbalance in outcome measures, which heavily rely on the Mayo score while underutilizing patient-reported outcomes and novel endoscopic scoring tools.
CONCLUSION: The number of clinical trials for active ulcerative colitis has increased, and intervention strategies have become more varied. However, there is significant variation in study populations, trial design, and the evaluation of their effectiveness. Future trials should prioritize large-scale, long-term studies with comprehensive and patient-centered outcome measures.

papers.title: ECCO Topical Review on Optimisation of Therapy for Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.authors: Ernest-Suarez K, Ungar B, Katsanos K, Lobatón T, Rodriguez-Lago I, Yanai H
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Advanced therapies have revolutionized inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) management, but primary non-response and secondary loss of response remain clinical challenges across all mechanisms of action. This topical review aims to offer evidence-based current practice positions for therapy optimization across all available advanced therapies.
METHODS: A panel of gastroenterologists performed a literature review on optimization of IBD advanced therapies (anti-tumour necrosis factor agents, vedolizumab, anti-IL-12/23 and anti-IL-23 agents, and small molecules) and formulated current practice positions that were approved in consensus.
CONCLUSIONS: Strategies to reduce treatment failures, maximize drug persistence, and achieve optimal clinical benefit, including therapeutic drug monitoring and dose optimization, have become standard components of modern IBD care; however, this may vary according to the current evidence for each specific drug.

papers.title: XIAP induces inflammation and promotes colorectal cancer progression
papers.authors: Schiffmann L, Daoud M, Wunderlich C, Schorn F, Stachelscheid J, Broxtermann P
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most diagnosed malignancies worldwide, with chronic inflammation playing a critical role in its pathogenesis and progression. Surgery represents the primary treatment option, though some patients suffer from relapse, leading to considerable morbidity and mortality. A better molecular understanding of CRC pathogenesis is therefore essential for identifying patients at increased risk of recurrence and improving clinical management. Here we identified the X-linked inhibitor of apoptosis protein (XIAP) as an independent predictor of overall survival in primary resected CRC patients. To model CRC patients with low versus high XIAP expression, we established conditional mouse lines for intestinal epithelial cell (IECs)-specific Xiap knock-out and XIAP knock-in, and employed a colitis-associated murine model for CRC. We found that XIAP promotes inflammatory signalling and exacerbates colitis-driven colorectal tumorigenesis by shaping a distinct tumor inflammatory microenvironment characterized by increased immune-cell infiltration, including neutrophils, and enhanced vascularisation. The pro-inflammatory role of XIAP was further validated in CRC patient-derived organoids and human CRC tumor specimens. Collectively, our findings identify XIAP as a potential biomarker of CRC-associated inflammation and a candidate marker for identifying patients at increased risk of disease recurrence. Moreover, these results provide a rationale for exploring XIAP-targeting strategies as a potential component of multimodal therapeutic approaches for CRC.

papers.title: Inflammatory bowel disease and the heart: how trained immunity shapes cardiovascular outcomes
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), comprising Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is a chronic relapsing intestinal inflammatory disorder. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of death in patients with IBD, with elevated risks of myocardial infarction, heart failure, stroke, and venous thromboembolism that are independent of traditional risk factors. Disease activity and histological inflammation independently predict major adverse cardiovascular events, and Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis differ in cardiovascular risk profiles. This residual risk points to immune mechanisms that remain unclear. Trained immunity (TI), an innate immune memory induced by epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming, may link chronic intestinal inflammation to cardiovascular injury. This review integrates epidemiological and mechanistic evidence, outlines cardiovascular risk features in IBD, examines the molecular basis of TI and its roles in atherosclerosis, myocardial injury, and heart failure, and evaluates candidate biomarkers and targeted therapeutic strategies. We also discuss current limitations and challenges in clinical translation and propose future research directions, to inform mechanistic studies and clinical interventions for IBD-associated CVD.

papers.title: Context-dependent cGAS-STING signaling in solid tumors: biological determinants, clinical implications, and biomarker-guided therapeutic strategies
papers.authors: Wang Z, Yu Y, Zhu Y
papers.abstract: Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) agonists are intended to convert cytosolic DNA sensing into productive antitumor immunity, yet their biological effects vary substantially among tumors. Outcomes depend on the cellular compartment engaged, the amplitude and duration of signaling, tumor genotype, the immune architecture of the tumor microenvironment, and drug distribution. A critical distinction must therefore be made between chronic endogenous, tumor-cell-intrinsic cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) signaling, as may occur in chromosomally unstable tumors, and controlled pharmacological STING agonism. The former can sustain maladaptive inflammatory programs in selected experimental settings, whereas the latter can be delivered transiently and may preferentially activate dendritic cells and other host immune compartments. This narrative review examines canonical STING-TBK1-IRF3/type I interferon signaling and alternative chronic outputs; relates these mechanisms to chromosomal instability, mismatch-repair status, immune surveillance, and immune checkpoint blockade; and evaluates early clinical experience with intratumoral STING agonists. Available trials demonstrate target engagement and generally manageable toxicity, but efficacy has been limited or heterogeneous. Mismatch-repair status, tumor mutational burden, chromosomal instability, baseline interferon activity, STING pathway competence, immune-cell topology, and delivery feasibility should therefore be considered components of a candidate composite biomarker strategy rather than validated predictors. By contrast, STING inhibition in chromosomal-instability-high tumors remains a promising preclinical hypothesis, not an established treatment. Prospective, compartment-resolved biomarker studies are needed to match agonists, delivery systems, combination regimens, or inhibitory approaches to the appropriate tumor state.

papers.title: Ultrasound-responsive nanoplatforms for cancer immunotherapy: engineering spatiotemporal immune activation in the tumor microenvironment
papers.authors: Zhang Q, Wei T, Lan Z, Lin G, Xu M, Li X
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has reshaped cancer therapy, but durable responses remain limited by insufficient antigen release, poor T-cell infiltration, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments, and systemic immune-related toxicity. Ultrasound-responsive nanoplatforms provide a spatiotemporally controllable strategy to overcome these barriers by exploiting deep tissue penetration, focal activation, and repeatable external triggering. In this review, we summarize recent experimental advances in sonosensitizer-based and ultrasound-triggered nanoplatforms for cancer immunotherapy. These systems integrate sonodynamic immunogenic cell death, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, necroptosis, cGAS-STING activation, immune checkpoint blockade, mRNA delivery, gas therapy, and tumor microenvironment remodeling to convert immune-cold tumors into immune-responsive lesions. We further discuss cancer type-specific applications in hepatocellular carcinoma, pancreatic cancer, glioblastoma, triple-negative breast cancer, colorectal cancer, bladder cancer, and other solid tumors, emphasizing how ultrasound-responsive designs can be matched to distinct anatomical and immunological barriers. Finally, we highlight key translational challenges, including long-term biosafety, controllable immune activation, ultrasound parameter standardization, scalable manufacturing, and clinically compatible combination strategies. Ultrasound-responsive nanoplatforms are emerging not merely as drug carriers, but as programmable immune-engineering systems capable of coordinating when, where, and how antitumor immunity is activated within the tumor microenvironment.

papers.title: Dietary exposures, microbial ecology and carcinogenesis: An integrated review
papers.authors: Kang J, Soh W, Wong S
papers.abstract: The gut microbiome can influence cancer susceptibility, progression, and treatment response. Microbes shape carcinogenesis through direct genotoxicity, epithelial barrier disruption, sustained inflammation, immune modulation, and the biotransformation of diet-derived substrates into bioactive metabolites. Diet is an important modifiable determinant of microbial community composition and function: Western dietary patterns may favour pro-carcinogenic microbial activities, whereas plant-rich, fibre-dense diets can support saccharolytic fermentation and commensal functions. These effects depend on substrate availability, microbial strain and host context. This review centres on colorectal and gastric cancers, with selected evidence from hepatocellular, pancreatic, breast and head-and-neck malignancies. Establishing causality remains central: most human evidence is associative, and mechanistic or interventional evidence is required for therapeutic or preventive translation. This review summarises the mechanistic roles of specific bacterial pathobionts, commensals and fungi across these cancer types, distinguishes observational, experimental and clinical interventional evidence for diet-microbiome interactions, and identifies translational priorities.

papers.title: Bugs and drugs: The interplay between IBD therapeutics, inflammation and the gut microbiome - implications for colonic carcinogenesis
papers.authors: Messiha K, Khan S, Houshyar Y, Damm G, Hold G
papers.abstract: With the rising global prevalence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and improved patient longevity, the burden of colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CAC) is increasing. Patients with IBD have a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC) compared with the general population and are typically diagnosed at a younger age than those with sporadic CRC. This elevated risk is driven by chronic and recurrent inflammatory injury to the intestinal mucosa, which plays a central mechanistic role in carcinogenesis. In contrast to the adenoma-carcinoma sequence observed in sporadic CRC, CAC arises through a distinct inflammation-dysplasia-carcinoma pathway with persistent inflammation initiating and promoting tumorigenesis. Evidence strongly implicates the gut microbiota as being a risk factor in both IBD and CRC. This review synthesises current evidence on the role of the gut microbiota across IBD, CRC and CAC, with a particular focus on the impact of IBD therapeutics on colitis-associated carcinogenesis and the intersection with gut microbiota changes. We identify critical gaps in mechanistic understanding and emphasise the urgent need for mechanism-driven, personalised strategies to enable meaningful clinical translation.

papers.title: Fusobacterium nucleatum in cancer: prognostic relevance and clinical implications
papers.authors: Lehr K, Thon C, Link A
papers.abstract: Fusobacterium nucleatum (F. nucleatum) is a Gram-negative anaerobic bacterium of the normal human microbiota, originally identified in the oral cavity but now recognised as a constituent of the intratumoural microbiome across a broad range of human malignancies. This structured narrative review summarises the human evidence for F. nucleatum in different tumour entities. Within little more than a decade, F. nucleatum has become one of the most extensively characterised tumour-associated bacteria. Its DNA has been detected in every entity covered here, and in colorectal cancer a substantial and reproducible body of work links intratumoural F. nucleatum to shorter survival across independent cohorts, populations and detection platforms, increasingly resolved to subspecies and clade level. Evidence in other entities is younger and more heterogeneous: several show comparable associations, whereas in oral squamous cell carcinoma F. nucleatum positivity has been linked to improved outcomes. Rather than undermining the field, this heterogeneity points to a context-dependent biology shaped by tumour type and molecular subtype, specimen, detection method and threshold, and treatment setting. Mechanistic work provides a coherent basis for these observations. In experimental models, the adhesins FadA and Fap2 mediate interactions with host cells that promote proliferative signalling, immune evasion and metastatic spread, and bacterial depletion attenuates tumour growth - proof of principle for a targetable microbial component of the tumour. F. nucleatum is therefore a compelling candidate for microbiome-informed oncology. Realising this potential requires standardised assays, validated cut-offs and prospective trials.

papers.title: Aging and the Microbiome: precondition for gastrointestinal carcinogenesis
papers.abstract: This review summarizes how aging-related changes in the gut microbiome contribute to gastrointestinal carcinogenesis. We highlight that cancer risk in aging is shaped not only by chronological age but largely by diet, lifestyle, environment, and their impact on microbial ecology. In healthy aging, microbial diversity is preserved with functional redundancy among short-chain fatty acid-producing commensals that support barrier integrity, immune regulation, and metabolic homeostasis. In unhealthy aging, loss of beneficial taxa, expansion of pathobionts, and accumulation of pro-inflammatory and genotoxic metabolites promote chronic inflammation, epithelial dysfunction, and DNA damage, thereby facilitating tumour development. Key microbial drivers include pks + Escherichia coli, enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis, and Fusobacterium nucleatum, acting through genotoxic, inflammatory, and immune-evasive mechanisms. Although microbiome-targeted interventions such as diet modification, probiotics, faecal microbiota transfer, and phage-based strategies are promising, current evidence remains largely preclinical or observational. Overall, the gut microbiome is a central, modifiable mediator of aging-associated gastrointestinal cancer risk, but longitudinal studies are needed to establish causality and therapeutic efficacy.

papers.title: Virome and colorectal cancer: Paving the way for future explorations and clinical applications
papers.authors: Ru J, Xue J, Chen Z, Deng L
papers.abstract: The pathogenesis of colorectal cancer (CRC) is inextricably linked to the gut microbiome. However, research has historically concentrated on the bacteriome, leaving the gut virome (predominantly composed of bacteriophages) largely unexplored as biological "dark matter". Recent advancements have illuminated the dual regulatory role of phages within the tumor microenvironment (TME), where they intricately modulate both bacterial community dynamics and host immune responses. This review synthesizes current evidence on viral dysbiosis throughout CRC progression and evaluates the translational potential of virome signatures as highly specific, non-invasive diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers. We then explore emerging virome-based interventions, including precision phage therapies, aimed at reshaping the TME and enhancing synergistic responses to conventional treatments and immunotherapy. To propel the field from correlative observations to actionable clinical applications, significant translational hurdles must be overcome. We highlight the urgent need for standardized bioinformatics pipelines to address reproducibility challenges and emphasize the utility of advanced, culture-independent methodologies like single-cell viral tagging to accurately map host-phage interaction networks. Finally, we advocate for the integration of large-animal models, such as CRC pig models, to validate the causal roles and longitudinal dynamics of the virome, ultimately bridging the gap between basic exploration and precision gastrointestinal oncology.
